record.context_brief: Aztec rectangle with the central square removed
record.original_question: Find a formula for the number of domino tilings of a 2n-by-(2n+1) Aztec rectangle after deleting its central square.

evidence.quote: One can also look at "Aztec rectangles" from which squares have been removed so as to restore the balance between black and white squares (a necessary condition for tilability). For instance, one can remove the central square from an a-by-b Aztec rectangle in which a and b differ by 1, with the larger of a, b odd:
Problem 9: Find a formula for the number of domino tilings of a 2n-by-(2n + 1) Aztec rectangle with its central square removed.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
An Aztec rectangle of dimensions $a \times b$ is a region of the square lattice consisting of unit cells whose centers $(i+\tfrac12, j+\tfrac12)$ satisfy appropriate inequalities so that the region is the union of $a$ rows and $b$ columns of cells with a "staircase" boundary in the style of the Aztec diamond. Specifically, color the unit squares of the standard square lattice in a checkerboard fashion. For positive integers $a < b$ with $b = a+1$, the $a \times b$ Aztec rectangle is the region tileable in principle by horizontal and vertical $1 \times 2$ dominoes (up to a defect in the balance of colors), having $a$ rows of cells and a staircase boundary; for the case $a = 2n$, $b = 2n+1$ this region has exactly one more square of one color than of the other, and a tiling by dominoes does not exist.

Now fix a positive integer $n$ and consider the $2n \times (2n+1)$ Aztec rectangle. Remove its central unit square (the unique cell of the majority color situated at the geometric center of the region), thereby restoring the balance between the two color classes (a necessary condition for the existence of a domino tiling).

Find a closed-form formula (a product formula or other explicit expression) for the number of domino tilings of the resulting region as a function of $n$.
artifact.status_search_result: Multiple secondary sources (including Tri Lai's survey/research statements and follow-up literature) indicate that this problem was solved by Harald Helfgott, following from the main result of his 1998 Brandeis senior thesis on edge effects in the Aztec diamond. The resulting count can be expressed as a determinant evaluation; explicit product-form expressions are noted to have nontrivial (not entirely smooth) prime factorizations.

status_evidence.title: Enumeration of Tilings and Related Problems (Tri Lai)
status_evidence.snippet: Problem 9 ... 2n-by-(2n+1) Aztec rectangle with its central square removed ... solved by Helfgott; follows from the main result of his thesis [1998].
status_evidence.claim: Problem 9 of Propp's list is solved by Helfgott's thesis.

status_evidence.title: Enumeration of Tilings of Diamonds and Hexagons with Defects (Helfgott–Gessel)
status_evidence.snippet: We use determinants to count tilings of Aztec diamonds and hexagons with defects ... solutions to several problems on Propp's list.
status_evidence.claim: Helfgott–Gessel methods produce determinant formulas for tilings of Aztec regions with defects, including Propp's problems.
